cards.front: Why is the org-ID naming quirk dangerous for queries?
cards.back: Send-time behaviour is fine ( latest record wins ), but a naive SELECT against the DMO returns both rows with no signal which one the platform acted on — unexplained duplicate rows in consent exports.
cards.frontHtml: Why is the org-ID naming quirk dangerous for queries?
cards.backHtml: Send-time behaviour is fine (latest record wins), but a naive SELECT against the DMO returns both rows with no signal which one the platform acted on — unexplained duplicate rows in consent exports.

cards.front: Why is no consent DLO name portable?
cards.back: The org ID is appended to the stream name, so the name differs per org (and changes when the org ID changes). Nothing that references the consent DLO by name is portable — not a Data Transform, saved query, Calculated Insight, or runbook.
cards.frontHtml: Why is no consent DLO name portable?
cards.backHtml: The org ID is appended to the stream name, so the name differs per org (and changes when the org ID changes). Nothing that references the consent DLO by name is portable — not a Data Transform, saved query, Calculated Insight, or runbook.

cards.front: What are the key fields in the V2 consent stream → DMO mapping?
cards.back: ConsentId (primary key = contact point value + CSCT Id), ConsentCapturedDateTime (when the person decided) and UpdatedTime (when the row changed) as separate fields, and PartyId mapped to Party (carrying nothing). Ten fields mapped, seventeen left unmapped.
cards.frontHtml: What are the key fields in the V2 consent stream → DMO mapping?
cards.backHtml: ConsentId (primary key = contact point value + CSCT Id), ConsentCapturedDateTime (when the person decided) and UpdatedTime (when the row changed) as separate fields, and PartyId mapped to Party (carrying nothing). Ten fields mapped, seventeen left unmapped.

cards.front: What is the one rule governing consent writes?
cards.back: Only writes that go through the consent service count. The service writes into a DLO mapped to the CSC DMO and updates the cache. Everything else produces a row and changes nothing in the cache.
cards.frontHtml: What is the one rule governing consent writes?
cards.backHtml: Only writes that go through the consent service count. The service writes into a DLO mapped to the CSC DMO and updates the cache. Everything else produces a row and changes nothing in the cache.

cards.front: Name the supported consent write methods.
cards.back: Bulk CSV import (50k rows/file), Privacy Consent Status component, unsubscribe URLs / preference pages / SMS & WhatsApp opt-outs, landing page forms paired with an Automation Event-Triggered Flow, and the Consent Request / Create Consent flow action.
cards.frontHtml: Name the supported consent write methods.
cards.backHtml: Bulk CSV import (50k rows/file), Privacy Consent Status component, unsubscribe URLs / preference pages / SMS & WhatsApp opt-outs, landing page forms paired with an Automation Event-Triggered Flow, and the Consent Request / Create Consent flow action.

cards.front: When did the Consent Request element become available in Record-Triggered Flows?
cards.back: Winter '27 Release — with some orgs receiving the option before the official release window.
cards.frontHtml: When did the Consent Request element become available in Record-Triggered Flows?
cards.backHtml: Winter '27 Release — with some orgs receiving the option before the official release window.

cards.front: Name the unsupported consent write methods and why they fail.
cards.back: Data stream mapped directly to the consent DLO; Bulk Ingestion API writing to the consent DMO; Batch Data Transforms updating a mapped DLO; legacy MessagingConsent / MessagingConsentV2 flow actions; external systems writing into the consent DMO. All bypass the consent service .
cards.frontHtml: Name the unsupported consent write methods and why they fail.
cards.backHtml: Data stream mapped directly to the consent DLO; Bulk Ingestion API writing to the consent DMO; Batch Data Transforms updating a mapped DLO; legacy MessagingConsent/MessagingConsentV2 flow actions; external systems writing into the consent DMO. All bypass the consent service.

cards.front: How does an unsupported write fail, and does anything error?
cards.back: It fails in both directions — an email may fail to send to an address that appears opted in, and may send to an address that appears opted out. The DMO can also disagree with the Privacy Consent Status component. Nothing errors anywhere.
cards.frontHtml: How does an unsupported write fail, and does anything error?
cards.backHtml: It fails in both directions — an email may fail to send to an address that appears opted in, and may send to an address that appears opted out. The DMO can also disagree with the Privacy Consent Status component. Nothing errors anywhere.

cards.front: How do you fix consent written through an unsupported path?
cards.back: There is no cache flush — re-issue every affected consent change through a supported method. Small sets: the component. Larger: a Data Cloud-Triggered Flow calling Create Consent across the affected population, or CSV import as a replay tool.
cards.frontHtml: How do you fix consent written through an unsupported path?
cards.backHtml: There is no cache flush — re-issue every affected consent change through a supported method. Small sets: the component. Larger: a Data Cloud-Triggered Flow calling Create Consent across the affected population, or CSV import as a replay tool.

cards.front: Where can you find consent data?
cards.back: On the record via the Privacy Consent Status component (Lead/Contact/Person Account); in Data Explorer against the CSC DMO (search on contact point value); in Query Editor for joins and audit-trail data (Data Explorer won't show the audit trail).
cards.frontHtml: Where can you find consent data?
cards.backHtml: On the record via the Privacy Consent Status component (Lead/Contact/Person Account); in Data Explorer against the CSC DMO (search on contact point value); in Query Editor for joins and audit-trail data (Data Explorer won't show the audit trail).

cards.front: What four things can you currently not see about consent?
cards.back: 1) The cache . 2) Who changed a record (no actor field). 3) Consent history on the record. 4) Anything in the Party field. (Plus: the component shows only the 100 most recent records.)
cards.frontHtml: What four things can you currently not see about consent?
cards.backHtml: 1) The cache. 2) Who changed a record (no actor field). 3) Consent history on the record. 4) Anything in the Party field. (Plus: the component shows only the 100 most recent records.)

cards.front: How long do consent changes take to appear in the DMO?
cards.back: Minutes — long enough that a test looks like it failed when it has only just started, and long enough that people retry the write and create a second problem. With Consent Changes in flows, up to a couple of hours.
cards.frontHtml: How long do consent changes take to appear in the DMO?
cards.backHtml: Minutes — long enough that a test looks like it failed when it has only just started, and long enough that people retry the write and create a second problem. With Consent Changes in flows, up to a couple of hours.

cards.front: How do you undo a bad initial consent import?
cards.back: You can't self-serve — audit trail rows cannot be deleted through any self-service route , so it means opening a case with Salesforce Support. Plan the initial import as if you cannot undo it.
cards.frontHtml: How do you undo a bad initial consent import?
cards.backHtml: You can't self-serve — audit trail rows cannot be deleted through any self-service route, so it means opening a case with Salesforce Support. Plan the initial import as if you cannot undo it.

cards.front: What is the unresolved question about the 90-day cache clock?
cards.back: Whether it runs from the write or the last read , and whether a send refreshes the entry. If it resets on read, 90 days is a floor rather than a ceiling .
cards.frontHtml: What is the unresolved question about the 90-day cache clock?
cards.backHtml: Whether it runs from the write or the last read, and whether a send refreshes the entry. If it resets on read, 90 days is a floor rather than a ceiling.

cards.front: What is the unresolved question about merging Contacts?
cards.back: What happens to consent when two Contacts with different email addresses are merged. Nothing in the documentation covers it, and it matters to anyone running deduplication at scale.
cards.frontHtml: What is the unresolved question about merging Contacts?

cards.front: Name the five Data 360 segment types and their primary job.
cards.back: Standard (scheduled audience on a DMO), Real-Time (millisecond on-demand), Waterfall (priority-ranked mutually-exclusive offers), Dynamic (parameterized query, no persistence), Data Kit (predefined segment).
cards.frontHtml: Name the five Data 360 segment types and their primary job.
cards.backHtml: Standard (scheduled audience on a DMO), Real-Time (millisecond on-demand), Waterfall (priority-ranked mutually-exclusive offers), Dynamic (parameterized query, no persistence), Data Kit (predefined segment).

cards.front: What's the default lookback window, and its maximum?
cards.back: Default 90 days; up to 2 years (or 360 days via the "Days" dropdown). Container criteria can override the segment-level window.
cards.frontHtml: What's the default lookback window, and its maximum?
cards.backHtml: Default 90 days; up to 2 years (or 360 days via the "Days" dropdown). Container criteria can override the segment-level window.

cards.front: What's the maximum number of segments per org?
cards.frontHtml: What's the maximum number of segments per org?

cards.front: What can't a real-time segment do?
cards.back: Use exclusion criteria, nested batch segments, segment counts, or manual publish. (Requires Segment ID + Timestamp fields in the real-time data graph.)
cards.frontHtml: What can't a real-time segment do?
cards.backHtml: Use exclusion criteria, nested batch segments, segment counts, or manual publish. (Requires Segment ID + Timestamp fields in the real-time data graph.)

cards.front: What problem does a waterfall segment solve?
cards.back: It processes segments in priority order so a customer matching multiple segments is placed only in the highest-priority one — creating mutually exclusive audiences (one offer per person).
cards.frontHtml: What problem does a waterfall segment solve?
cards.backHtml: It processes segments in priority order so a customer matching multiple segments is placed only in the highest-priority one — creating mutually exclusive audiences (one offer per person).

cards.front: What are three key waterfall segment constraints?
cards.back: Max 20 segments; a segment can exist in only one waterfall (no nested segments); rapid publish not available.
cards.frontHtml: What are three key waterfall segment constraints?
cards.backHtml: Max 20 segments; a segment can exist in only one waterfall (no nested segments); rapid publish not available.

cards.front: How is a dynamic segment run, and why?
cards.back: Via API call through a broadcast flow supplying runtime values — because it uses placeholders and doesn't persist data in Segment Membership DMOs (can't be scheduled/published via UI).
cards.frontHtml: How is a dynamic segment run, and why?
cards.backHtml: Via API call through a broadcast flow supplying runtime values — because it uses placeholders and doesn't persist data in Segment Membership DMOs (can't be scheduled/published via UI).

cards.front: What are the standard and rapid publish intervals?
cards.back: Standard = 12 or 24 hours; Rapid = 1 or 4 hours (Marketing Cloud Engagement / file storage targets only).
cards.frontHtml: What are the standard and rapid publish intervals?
cards.backHtml: Standard = 12 or 24 hours; Rapid = 1 or 4 hours (Marketing Cloud Engagement / file storage targets only).

cards.front: How many rapid-publish segments can you create, and can you convert standard → rapid?
cards.back: Up to 20 rapid-publish segments; you cannot change a standard publish to rapid publish after creation.
cards.frontHtml: How many rapid-publish segments can you create, and can you convert standard → rapid?
cards.backHtml: Up to 20 rapid-publish segments; you cannot change a standard publish to rapid publish after creation.

cards.front: What do the "Latest" and "History" segment membership DMOs store?
cards.back: Latest = profiles in the most recent publish; History = prior publish (last 30 days), with Delta Type marking New/Existing/Removed.
cards.frontHtml: What do the "Latest" and "History" segment membership DMOs store?
cards.backHtml: Latest = profiles in the most recent publish; History = prior publish (last 30 days), with Delta Type marking New/Existing/Removed.

cards.front: Why should you "stop the publish schedule" instead of deactivating a segment you might reuse?
cards.back: Deactivation is permanent (can't be re-enabled); stopping the schedule preserves the segment for future use.
cards.frontHtml: Why should you "stop the publish schedule" instead of deactivating a segment you might reuse?
cards.backHtml: Deactivation is permanent (can't be re-enabled); stopping the schedule preserves the segment for future use.

cards.front: Why do composite keys cause problems in the Segment Canvas?
cards.back: The canvas joins on single-field relationships; composite keys only work in manual queries where every field is explicitly defined. Use DMOs with a single unique primary key.
cards.frontHtml: Why do composite keys cause problems in the Segment Canvas?
cards.backHtml: The canvas joins on single-field relationships; composite keys only work in manual queries where every field is explicitly defined. Use DMOs with a single unique primary key.

cards.front: What's the difference between a direct and a related attribute?
cards.back: Direct = single data point (postal code, name; 1:1 or N:1); related = collection of data points (purchase history; 1:N, often behavioral).
cards.frontHtml: What's the difference between a direct and a related attribute?
cards.backHtml: Direct = single data point (postal code, name; 1:1 or N:1); related = collection of data points (purchase history; 1:N, often behavioral).

cards.front: How do same-container vs. separate-container attributes behave?
cards.back: Same container = AND on the same row (single record); separate containers = independent filters (bought any X AND any Y).
cards.frontHtml: How do same-container vs. separate-container attributes behave?
cards.backHtml: Same container = AND on the same row (single record); separate containers = independent filters (bought any X AND any Y).

cards.front: What are the five aggregation types?
cards.back: Count, Sum, Average, Max, Min.
cards.frontHtml: What are the five aggregation types?
cards.backHtml: Count, Sum, Average, Max, Min.

cards.front: What are the filter/attribute/container limits in the segment canvas?
cards.back: 50 filters per tab (Include/Exclude), 100 attributes per segment, 20 filters per container.
cards.frontHtml: What are the filter/attribute/container limits in the segment canvas?
cards.backHtml: 50 filters per tab (Include/Exclude), 100 attributes per segment, 20 filters per container.

cards.front: What are the nesting limits?
cards.back: Up to 3 levels within a container; up to 10 levels across containers.
cards.frontHtml: What are the nesting limits?
cards.backHtml: Up to 3 levels within a container; up to 10 levels across containers.

cards.front: What three steps make up Group/Rank/Limit?
cards.back: (1) Group By a shared attribute, (2) Sort By an attribute with order, (3) Limit the maximum records per group.
cards.frontHtml: What three steps make up Group/Rank/Limit?
cards.backHtml: (1) Group By a shared attribute, (2) Sort By an attribute with order, (3) Limit the maximum records per group.

cards.front: What are two constraints on grouping/ranking/limiting rules?
cards.back: Max 3 group + 3 sort rules per ruleset; applies only within qualified profiles (not global), and only to direct attributes.
cards.frontHtml: What are two constraints on grouping/ranking/limiting rules?
cards.backHtml: Max 3 group + 3 sort rules per ruleset; applies only within qualified profiles (not global), and only to direct attributes.

cards.front: How are object joins and value matching case-sensitive?
cards.back: Object joins are case-sensitive (c12d3 ≠ C12D3); queries honor exact matching (accents, leading zeros) but text operators are case-insensitive.
cards.frontHtml: How are object joins and value matching case-sensitive?
cards.backHtml: Object joins are case-sensitive (c12d3 ≠ C12D3); queries honor exact matching (accents, leading zeros) but text operators are case-insensitive.

cards.front: What is the Approximate Segment Population field?
cards.back: A 95%-confidence range estimate of the population (enable in Feature Manager); less accurate for small populations or low Segment On counts.
cards.frontHtml: What is the Approximate Segment Population field?
cards.backHtml: A 95%-confidence range estimate of the population (enable in Feature Manager); less accurate for small populations or low Segment On counts.

cards.front: What does an attribute shortcut store, and what's its limit?
cards.back: Segment-on object + object path + target attribute (reusable filter); limit 500 per tenant, scoped to data space.
cards.frontHtml: What does an attribute shortcut store, and what's its limit?
cards.backHtml: Segment-on object + object path + target attribute (reusable filter); limit 500 per tenant, scoped to data space.

cards.front: What does hierarchical aggregation do, and on which entities?
cards.back: Rolls up revenues across account hierarchies (parent/subsidiary); supported on Account/Unified Account, up to 5 containers and 3 levels per DMO.
cards.frontHtml: What does hierarchical aggregation do, and on which entities?
cards.backHtml: Rolls up revenues across account hierarchies (parent/subsidiary); supported on Account/Unified Account, up to 5 containers and 3 levels per DMO.

cards.front: How far back can an Engagement DMO's event date field go in a segment?
cards.back: Up to 24 months; a segment fails if the date range exceeds this.
cards.frontHtml: How far back can an Engagement DMO's event date field go in a segment?
cards.backHtml: Up to 24 months; a segment fails if the date range exceeds this.

cards.front: What are the value limits of the Is In operator?
cards.back: Up to 100 comma-separated values (bulk paste up to 10,000 via import).
cards.frontHtml: What are the value limits of the Is In operator?
cards.backHtml: Up to 100 comma-separated values (bulk paste up to 10,000 via import).

cards.front: What two prerequisites must be met before creating an Einstein segment?
cards.back: A completed identity resolution ruleset creating a Unified Individual DMO with ≥10 records, and enabling generative AI + Einstein Segment Creation in Feature Manager.
cards.frontHtml: What two prerequisites must be met before creating an Einstein segment?
cards.backHtml: A completed identity resolution ruleset creating a Unified Individual DMO with ≥10 records, and enabling generative AI + Einstein Segment Creation in Feature Manager.

cards.front: How does Einstein Segment Creation reduce bias and improve accuracy?
cards.back: Demographic attributes are removed by default, and attributes producing fewer than 10 results are stripped.
cards.frontHtml: How does Einstein Segment Creation reduce bias and improve accuracy?
cards.backHtml: Demographic attributes are removed by default, and attributes producing fewer than 10 results are stripped.

cards.front: What does Einstein Data Prism do?
cards.back: Grounds generative AI by scanning metadata (schema, relationships, sample values, descriptions), auto-generating descriptions, and returning focused grounding data for natural-language queries.
cards.frontHtml: What does Einstein Data Prism do?
cards.backHtml: Grounds generative AI by scanning metadata (schema, relationships, sample values, descriptions), auto-generating descriptions, and returning focused grounding data for natural-language queries.

cards.front: What does Metadata Studio let you do?
cards.back: Validate/edit object+field descriptions and exclude irrelevant entities so they aren't sent to the LLM or used for grounding.
cards.frontHtml: What does Metadata Studio let you do?
cards.backHtml: Validate/edit object+field descriptions and exclude irrelevant entities so they aren't sent to the LLM or used for grounding.

cards.front: Where are Einstein Data Prism and Metadata Studio unsupported?
cards.back: Government Cloud Plus — don't enable the feature there.
cards.frontHtml: Where are Einstein Data Prism and Metadata Studio unsupported?
cards.backHtml: Government Cloud Plus — don't enable the feature there.

cards.front: When are segmentation credits consumed?
cards.back: On segment publish (Data Services "Segmentation" / Flex Credits "Data 360 Segmentation"), plus Data Queries for counting/building/previewing.
cards.frontHtml: When are segmentation credits consumed?
cards.backHtml: On segment publish (Data Services "Segmentation" / Flex Credits "Data 360 Segmentation"), plus Data Queries for counting/building/previewing.

cards.front: Is Agentforce Marketing a product? What is it?
cards.back: It's not a single product — it's the broader brand of Salesforce's next-generation marketing portfolio. Marketing Cloud Next is just one product inside it.
cards.frontHtml: Is Agentforce Marketing a product? What is it?
cards.backHtml: It's not a single product — it's the broader brand of Salesforce's next-generation marketing portfolio. Marketing Cloud Next is just one product inside it.

cards.front: Name the four products in the Agentforce Marketing portfolio and what each evolved from.
cards.back: Marketing Cloud Next (evolution of Marketing Cloud Engagement) · Salesforce Personalization (evolution of Marketing Cloud Personalization, real-time) · Marketing Intelligence (evolution of Marketing Cloud Intelligence, AI-powered analytics) · Loyalty Management (no-code B2B/B2C loyalty & rewards).

cards.front: What two editions does Marketing Cloud Next offer, and how do they relate?
cards.back: Growth Edition and Advanced Edition . Advanced includes all Growth capabilities plus additional features. The list isn't exhaustive — new capabilities arrive each release.

cards.front: Which scoring types are available in which editions?

cards.front: How does Salesforce frame the Marketing Cloud Next setup process?
cards.back: As configuration rather than implementation — MC Next and Data 360 can be enabled in just a few clicks with a setup interface guiding you through the process.

cards.front: At a minimum, how many key configuration steps are there, and what are the first three?
cards.back: Six key steps (plus optional ones not required for core functionality). The first three — driven by the Setup Assistant — are: set up Data 360 , enable Marketing Cloud , and deploy the required data streams .

cards.front: Which two permission sets must a System Administrator-profile user assign before anyone configures MC Next?
cards.back: Data Cloud Architect (Data 360 setup, data modelling objects, install data kits, deploy streams, configure identity resolution) and Marketing Admin (configure most marketing settings in Setup, publish/activate campaigns and segments).

cards.front: After the Setup Assistant completes, what two additional required tasks remain?
cards.back: 1) Add the company's physical address to the Company Information page (included in the footer of promotional emails for regulatory compliance). 2) Create an authenticated domain .

cards.front: How does domain setup differ between Marketing Cloud Engagement and Marketing Cloud Next?
cards.back: MCE uses a sender authentication package to configure the sending domain and branded account domains. MC Next has you add an authenticated domain , generate the required DNS records , and publish them through your DNS provider.
cards.frontHtml: How does domain setup differ between Marketing Cloud Engagement and Marketing Cloud Next?

cards.front: What are the steps to add an authenticated domain in MC Next?
cards.back: Setup → Quick Find "Authenticated Domains" → Add Domain → Continue → define the subdomain → create a default From email username → download a DNS zone file or view individual DNS records → add them at your DNS provider → tick the confirmation checkbox → Activate My Domain .
cards.frontHtml: What are the steps to add an authenticated domain in MC Next?
cards.backHtml: Setup → Quick Find "Authenticated Domains" → Add Domain → Continue → define the subdomain → create a default From email username → download a DNS zone file or view individual DNS records → add them at your DNS provider → tick the confirmation checkbox → Activate My Domain.

cards.front: What's the difference between an authorized email domain and an authenticated domain?
cards.back: An authorized email domain verifies ownership with a simple verification record and does not provide the complete DKIM/DNS sending configuration. An authenticated domain establishes the full DKIM and DNS sending configuration. Authorized domains are required for dynamic From or Reply-to addresses .

An authenticated domain establishes the full DKIM and DNS sending configuration. Authorized domains are required for dynamic From or Reply-to addresses.

cards.front: What causes a DMARC alignment failure with From addresses?
cards.back: For DMARC alignment, the domain in the From address must align with the authenticated sending domain . Using a personal email address on the root domain as the From address may result in DMARC alignment failures.
cards.frontHtml: What causes a DMARC alignment failure with From addresses?

cards.front: Name the four levels of attributing consent to promotional communications.
cards.back: Level 1 = the entire individual record (all channels/subscriptions/contact points). Level 2 = a communication channel as a whole (e.g., all email). Level 3 = a specific contact point value (email/phone), regardless of subscription. Level 4 = a specific contact point and a specific subscription type.
cards.frontHtml: Name the four levels of attributing consent to promotional communications.
cards.backHtml: Level 1 = the entire individual record (all channels/subscriptions/contact points). Level 2 = a communication channel as a whole (e.g., all email). Level 3 = a specific contact point value (email/phone), regardless of subscription. Level 4 = a specific contact point and a specific subscription type.

cards.front: Which consent level does Marketing Cloud Next enforce?
cards.back: Level 4 — the most granular level, applying to a specific contact point (email address or phone number) and a specific subscription type.
cards.frontHtml: Which consent level does Marketing Cloud Next enforce?
cards.backHtml: Level 4 — the most granular level, applying to a specific contact point (email address or phone number) and a specific subscription type.

cards.front: Name the four objects that manage Level 4 consent and what each represents.
cards.back: Communication Subscription (the type/purpose/category of communication) · Communication Subscription Channel Type (the channel used to deliver a subscription) · Communication Subscription Consent (the individual's consent status for a subscription at a specific contact point value + subscription channel type) · Engagement Channel Type (the channel: email, SMS, WhatsApp, RCS).
cards.frontHtml: Name the four objects that manage Level 4 consent and what each represents.
cards.backHtml: Communication Subscription (the type/purpose/category of communication) · Communication Subscription Channel Type (the channel used to deliver a subscription) · Communication Subscription Consent (the individual's consent status for a subscription at a specific contact point value + subscription channel type) · Engagement Channel Type (the channel: email, SMS, WhatsApp, RCS).

cards.front: Give a concrete example of what a Communication Subscription Consent record stores.
cards.back: Someone at example.com opted into Marketing via email — i.e., a contact point value + subscription + channel combination.
cards.frontHtml: Give a concrete example of what a Communication Subscription Consent record stores.

cards.front: What are the limitations of the consent file import?
cards.back: It's a manual, user-driven process; each file is limited to 50,000 rows ; each upload covers one channel , applies to one subscription , and assigns one consent status (opt-in or opt-out).
cards.frontHtml: What are the limitations of the consent file import?

cards.front: In which flow types is the Create Consent element available, and what is it called in each?
cards.back: Available in Automation Event-Triggered Flows , On-Demand Flows , and Data Cloud-Triggered Flows . In Automation Event-Triggered and On-Demand flows it's labelled Consent Request ; in Data Cloud-Triggered flows it's Create Consent .
cards.frontHtml: In which flow types is the Create Consent element available, and what is it called in each?
cards.backHtml: Available in Automation Event-Triggered Flows, On-Demand Flows, and Data Cloud-Triggered Flows. In Automation Event-Triggered and On-Demand flows it's labelled Consent Request; in Data Cloud-Triggered flows it's Create Consent.

cards.front: Name the four unsupported methods for updating consent.
cards.back: Batch Data Transform , direct mapping from a data stream , bulk ingestion using the Bulk Ingestion API , and the MessagingConsentV2 flow action . They can materialize records from a DLO into the CSC DMO, but aren't supported consent management methods.
cards.frontHtml: Name the four unsupported methods for updating consent.
cards.backHtml: Batch Data Transform, direct mapping from a data stream, bulk ingestion using the Bulk Ingestion API, and the MessagingConsentV2 flow action. They can materialize records from a DLO into the CSC DMO, but aren't supported consent management methods.

cards.front: How long can it take for a consent record created via a data stream to materialise in the CSC DMO?
cards.back: Approximately 15 minutes — records ingested through data streams aren't available in the DMO in real time.
cards.frontHtml: How long can it take for a consent record created via a data stream to materialise in the CSC DMO?
cards.backHtml: Approximately 15 minutes — records ingested through data streams aren't available in the DMO in real time.

cards.front: Why did Salesforce build a caching layer into the consent service?
cards.back: To provide read-after-write consistency for consent updates — so the latest consent status is immediately available rather than waiting for the DMO to refresh.
cards.frontHtml: Why did Salesforce build a caching layer into the consent service?
cards.backHtml: To provide read-after-write consistency for consent updates — so the latest consent status is immediately available rather than waiting for the DMO to refresh.

cards.front: What is the time-to-live of a consent cache entry?
cards.back: 90 days , after which it expires automatically.
cards.frontHtml: What is the time-to-live of a consent cache entry?
cards.backHtml: 90 days, after which it expires automatically.

cards.front: When a consent record is created through the consent service, what order do things happen in?
cards.back: The cache is updated first (making the latest status immediately available), then the record is written to the underlying DLO , and the CSC DMO is later hydrated with the updated record.
cards.frontHtml: When a consent record is created through the consent service, what order do things happen in?
cards.backHtml: The cache is updated first (making the latest status immediately available), then the record is written to the underlying DLO, and the CSC DMO is later hydrated with the updated record.

cards.front: At send time, how does the send engine decide which consent value to use?
cards.back: It looks at the cache first . If there's no value for a contact point value, it looks at the value in the CSC DMO and then updates the cache. If a value is in the cache, it does not look at the DMO.
cards.frontHtml: At send time, how does the send engine decide which consent value to use?
cards.backHtml: It looks at the cache first. If there's no value for a contact point value, it looks at the value in the CSC DMO and then updates the cache. If a value is in the cache, it does not look at the DMO.

cards.front: Walk through the scenario where an opt-out is ignored at send time.
cards.back: 1) A consent record is created (opt-in) and materialised in the DMO via an unsupported method (e.g., direct data stream mapping). 2) An email is sent — no prior cache entry, so the cache is populated with the current (opt-in) status. 3) An opt-out record is streamed to the consent DLO — but there's no automatic cache update . 4) The next email sends because the cache still reports opt-in.
cards.frontHtml: Walk through the scenario where an opt-out is ignored at send time.
cards.backHtml: 1) A consent record is created (opt-in) and materialised in the DMO via an unsupported method (e.g., direct data stream mapping). 2) An email is sent — no prior cache entry, so the cache is populated with the current (opt-in) status. 3) An opt-out record is streamed to the consent DLO — but there's no automatic cache update. 4) The next email sends because the cache still reports opt-in.

cards.front: Why is there no automatic cache update when consent is written via a data stream mapping?
cards.back: Because there is currently no process that automatically updates an existing cache record when the status update is retrieved using a data stream mapping. Only supported write paths (which go through the consent service) refresh the cache.
cards.frontHtml: Why is there no automatic cache update when consent is written via a data stream mapping?
cards.backHtml: Because there is currently no process that automatically updates an existing cache record when the status update is retrieved using a data stream mapping. Only supported write paths (which go through the consent service) refresh the cache.

cards.front: How does the Create Consent element behave in a Data Cloud-Triggered Flow?
cards.back: When a change occurs on the contact point email DMO, the flow evaluates a condition (e.g., a consent status field updated). When satisfied, it triggers the consent action. When the flow interview reaches the action, consent values are written immediately to both the cache layer and the underlying DLO — so subsequent reads return the up-to-date status right away, before the DMO refreshes.
cards.frontHtml: How does the Create Consent element behave in a Data Cloud-Triggered Flow?
cards.backHtml: When a change occurs on the contact point email DMO, the flow evaluates a condition (e.g., a consent status field updated). When satisfied, it triggers the consent action. When the flow interview reaches the action, consent values are written immediately to both the cache layer and the underlying DLO — so subsequent reads return the up-to-date status right away, before the DMO refreshes.

cards.front: What did the Spring and Summer releases each add to preference pages?
cards.back: Spring: introduced custom preference pages . Summer: expanded to allow multiple preference pages (e.g., separate pages per brand).
cards.frontHtml: What did the Spring and Summer releases each add to preference pages?

cards.front: What can you configure when building a preference page?
cards.back: A brand (colours, typography, buttons, spacing, borders), content blocks (dividers, headings, lists, paragraphs), layouts , and image blocks — plus designate a default preference page used across all marketing message sends.

cards.front: How does the message channel affect which preference page is used?
cards.back: The channel automatically determines the page type: email messages link to the email preference manager ; SMS messages use a separate SMS-specific page. A unified email+SMS page isn't available out-of-the-box.
cards.frontHtml: How does the message channel affect which preference page is used?

cards.front: Name four limitations of out-of-the-box preference pages.
cards.back: No unified cross-channel page (needs custom development) · no native multilingual support (needs custom forms/development) · no custom code (AMPscript, Apex, server-side JavaScript) · can't pre-populate from URL parameters .

cards.front: What can't you edit in the standard subscription block, and what's the workaround?
cards.back: You can't edit button labels, headings, subheadings , or the order of the subscription list . Partial workaround: rename the communication subscriptions from the Consent tab . Full text customization is planned for an upcoming release.

cards.front: When you publish multiple preference pages, where do they appear?
cards.back: In the merge field selector , so you can choose the appropriate one when adding a preference page link to a message.

cards.back: Because the Communication Subscription Consent object in CRM is not the same object as the Communication Subscription Consent DMO — they're different halves of the model.

cards.front: How has the Data 360 dependency for audience data changed?
cards.back: Earlier releases required audience/decisioning/personalization data to exist in Data 360 . Spring '26 began reducing that dependency (CRM records as an audience source); Summer '26 went further (campaign members + actionable lists).

cards.back: You can use CRM records directly as an audience source — either on a scheduled basis or based on an event .

cards.front: What is an actionable list?
cards.back: A fixed (static) collection of audience members — useful when you already know exactly who you want to engage.

cards.front: How do you create an actionable list from a CSV import?

cards.back: Marketing Cloud Next does not automatically create corresponding consent records . Those consent records must be created or loaded separately — otherwise the audience is suppressed at send time (strict opt-in).

cards.front: What is the single orchestration engine for outbound messaging in MC Next, and how does that differ from MCE?
cards.back: Flow is the orchestration engine. In Marketing Cloud Engagement , messages could be sent from many tools/contexts (journeys, automations, triggered sends, UI sends, Salesforce sends, Content Builder sends). In MC Next, all outbound messaging is orchestrated through Flow .

cards.front: What are marketing flows also called, and how do they differ from core flows?
cards.back: Also called high-scale flows . They run on a separate high-scale processing engine and run off-core (outside the core Salesforce transactional runtime), so traditional governor-limit, transaction-management, and scaling concerns don't apply the same way .

cards.front: What are audience flows, and what do they unify?
cards.back: A Summer '26 concept that unifies several previously separate flow types into a single simplified orchestration experience — covering segments, actionable lists, CRM records, and campaign members . You choose the audience source directly in the flow configuration.
cards.frontHtml: What are audience flows, and what do they unify?
cards.backHtml: A Summer '26 concept that unifies several previously separate flow types into a single simplified orchestration experience — covering segments, actionable lists, CRM records, and campaign members. You choose the audience source directly in the flow configuration.

cards.front: What Journey Builder concept do audience flow re-entry conditions mirror?
cards.back: Journey Builder's contact entry mode . The three options are no re-entry , re-entry at any time , and re-entry only after exiting .
cards.frontHtml: What Journey Builder concept do audience flow re-entry conditions mirror?
cards.backHtml: Journey Builder's contact entry mode. The three options are no re-entry, re-entry at any time, and re-entry only after exiting.

cards.front: When were activation-triggered flows introduced, and what target type do they use?
cards.back: Winter '26 ; they use the Data 360 activation target type .
cards.frontHtml: When were activation-triggered flows introduced, and what target type do they use?
cards.backHtml: Winter '26; they use the Data 360 activation target type.

cards.front: What four things can you configure when creating an activation?
cards.back: Add filters to activation membership · add contact point filters · limit audience size based on attributes · append additional attributes from related objects associated with a segment member.
cards.frontHtml: What four things can you configure when creating an activation?
cards.backHtml: Add filters to activation membership · add contact point filters · limit audience size based on attributes · append additional attributes from related objects associated with a segment member.

cards.front: Why is the activation-as-personalization-source capability significant?
cards.back: Messages can use the activation directly as the personalization source , so email merge fields and repeaters can reference enriched Data 360 activation attributes — without additional lookups at send time .
cards.frontHtml: Why is the activation-as-personalization-source capability significant?
cards.backHtml: Messages can use the activation directly as the personalization source, so email merge fields and repeaters can reference enriched Data 360 activation attributes — without additional lookups at send time.

cards.front: What event sources can start an automation event-triggered flow?
cards.back: 1) Standard engagement events (email opens, clicks, form submissions — no extra config). 2) Engagement signals (custom events like website interactions, PDF downloads). 3) CRM record-triggered events (Spring '26 — prospect/lead/contact/related object created or updated).
cards.frontHtml: What event sources can start an automation event-triggered flow?
cards.backHtml: 1) Standard engagement events (email opens, clicks, form submissions — no extra config). 2) Engagement signals (custom events like website interactions, PDF downloads). 3) CRM record-triggered events (Spring '26 — prospect/lead/contact/related object created or updated).

cards.front: When were CRM record-triggered events introduced, and what fires them?
cards.back: Spring '26 . They fire when a prospect, lead, contact, or any related object record is created or updated.
cards.frontHtml: When were CRM record-triggered events introduced, and what fires them?
cards.backHtml: Spring '26. They fire when a prospect, lead, contact, or any related object record is created or updated.

cards.front: What are on-demand flows, and what makes them powerful?
cards.back: They let external systems trigger transactional messaging instantly through the REST API . Real-time personalization data can be passed directly in the API payload using an Apex-defined data schema — no need to ingest or hydrate data into Data Cloud first.
cards.frontHtml: What are on-demand flows, and what makes them powerful?
cards.backHtml: They let external systems trigger transactional messaging instantly through the REST API. Real-time personalization data can be passed directly in the API payload using an Apex-defined data schema — no need to ingest or hydrate data into Data Cloud first.

cards.front: What is the typical latency of an on-demand flow, and what is it ideal for?
cards.back: Approximately 1 to 3 seconds . Ideal for one-time passcodes, order confirmations, password resets, and real-time service alerts .
cards.frontHtml: What is the typical latency of an on-demand flow, and what is it ideal for?
cards.backHtml: Approximately 1 to 3 seconds. Ideal for one-time passcodes, order confirmations, password resets, and real-time service alerts.

cards.front: What two values are required in an on-demand flow API call, and what's the rule about the individual ID?
cards.back: Both the email address and individual ID are required. The individual ID doesn't need to correspond to an Individual record in Data 360 — it simply cannot be null . The request won't create an Individual DMO record, but engagement still appears in the Email Engagement DMO .
cards.frontHtml: What two values are required in an on-demand flow API call, and what's the rule about the individual ID?
cards.backHtml: Both the email address and individual ID are required. The individual ID doesn't need to correspond to an Individual record in Data 360 — it simply cannot be null. The request won't create an Individual DMO record, but engagement still appears in the Email Engagement DMO.

cards.front: What are broadcast flows designed for, and how do they differ from on-demand flows?
cards.back: Designed for fan-out processing — a single event triggers communication to a large group simultaneously . Both use the REST API, but on-demand targets an individual while broadcast targets all members of a segment .
cards.frontHtml: What are broadcast flows designed for, and how do they differ from on-demand flows?
cards.backHtml: Designed for fan-out processing — a single event triggers communication to a large group simultaneously. Both use the REST API, but on-demand targets an individual while broadcast targets all members of a segment.

cards.front: What segment type must a broadcast flow use, and when is it evaluated?
cards.back: A dynamic segment — evaluated at execution time using variables passed into the flow, allowing highly contextual audience resolution.
cards.frontHtml: What segment type must a broadcast flow use, and when is it evaluated?
cards.backHtml: A dynamic segment — evaluated at execution time using variables passed into the flow, allowing highly contextual audience resolution.

cards.front: Give three use cases for broadcast flows.
cards.back: Airline flight delay notifications · utility outage alerts · emergency notifications .
cards.frontHtml: Give three use cases for broadcast flows.
cards.backHtml: Airline flight delay notifications · utility outage alerts · emergency notifications.

cards.front: What happens when a broadcast flow API call executes?
cards.back: 1) The flow passes the parameter values required by the dynamic segment. 2) The segment refreshes and evaluates all individuals matching both static and dynamic criteria . 3) Every qualifying member is admitted into the flow . 4) Each recipient receives the personalized message.
cards.frontHtml: What happens when a broadcast flow API call executes?
cards.backHtml: 1) The flow passes the parameter values required by the dynamic segment. 2) The segment refreshes and evaluates all individuals matching both static and dynamic criteria. 3) Every qualifying member is admitted into the flow. 4) Each recipient receives the personalized message.

cards.front: Can broadcast flows run synchronously or asynchronously?
cards.back: Either , depending on the use case.
cards.frontHtml: Can broadcast flows run synchronously or asynchronously?
cards.backHtml: Either, depending on the use case.

cards.front: What triggers a Data Cloud-triggered flow, and how does it work under the hood?
cards.back: It executes when a record within a Data Cloud DMO (or Calculated Insight object ) is created or updated. Data 360 monitors the DMO ; when a matching change occurs, a data action publishes a platform event that triggers the flow.
cards.frontHtml: What triggers a Data Cloud-triggered flow, and how does it work under the hood?
cards.backHtml: It executes when a record within a Data Cloud DMO (or Calculated Insight object) is created or updated. Data 360 monitors the DMO; when a matching change occurs, a data action publishes a platform event that triggers the flow.

cards.front: Is a Data Cloud-triggered flow a marketing flow?
cards.back: ⚠️ Technically not — but it's still considered a high-scale flow type .
cards.frontHtml: Is a Data Cloud-triggered flow a marketing flow?
cards.backHtml: ⚠️ Technically not — but it's still considered a high-scale flow type.

cards.front: What is the most common use of a Data Cloud-triggered flow?
cards.back: Automating consent management based on DMO or Calculated Insight object record changes, using the Create Consent flow action — which updates the Communication Subscription DMO and the consent cache layer .
cards.frontHtml: What is the most common use of a Data Cloud-triggered flow?
cards.backHtml: Automating consent management based on DMO or Calculated Insight object record changes, using the Create Consent flow action — which updates the Communication Subscription DMO and the consent cache layer.

cards.front: Which two flow types cannot send emails from Marketing Cloud Next?
cards.back: Record-triggered flows (they're CRM flows) and Data Cloud-triggered (Data 360-triggered) flows .
cards.frontHtml: Which two flow types cannot send emails from Marketing Cloud Next?
cards.backHtml: Record-triggered flows (they're CRM flows) and Data Cloud-triggered (Data 360-triggered) flows.

cards.front: What does "off-core" mean, and what does it change?
cards.back: Marketing flows execute outside the core Salesforce transactional runtime on a separate high-scale engine. Because of this, traditional concerns around governor limits, transaction management, and scaling patterns don't apply in the same way .
cards.frontHtml: What does "off-core" mean, and what does it change?
cards.backHtml: Marketing flows execute outside the core Salesforce transactional runtime on a separate high-scale engine. Because of this, traditional concerns around governor limits, transaction management, and scaling patterns don't apply in the same way.

cards.front: How is personalization data supplied to on-demand and broadcast flow emails?
cards.back: Via an Apex class data provider — an Apex wrapper class defines the variables passed in the API payload, and the email uses the Apex class data provider to personalize content from those properties.
cards.frontHtml: How is personalization data supplied to on-demand and broadcast flow emails?
cards.backHtml: Via an Apex class data provider — an Apex wrapper class defines the variables passed in the API payload, and the email uses the Apex class data provider to personalize content from those properties.

cards.front: What does the "Available for Input" option do on a flow variable?
cards.back: It allows external systems to pass values into the flow through an API request — required for on-demand and broadcast flow variables supplied externally.
cards.frontHtml: What does the "Available for Input" option do on a flow variable?
cards.backHtml: It allows external systems to pass values into the flow through an API request — required for on-demand and broadcast flow variables supplied externally.

decks.title: Flashcards — Exam Masterclass Session 3 (Elliot Harper)
decks.meta: Source: sources/MCNext Consultant Exam Masterclass Session3.txt — the official Salesforce exam-prep masterclass, Session 3. Covers business units + Salesforce CMS, Marketing Workspaces, and the eight data providers for content personalization.
decks.metaHtml: Source: sources/MCNext_Consultant_Exam_Masterclass_Session3.txt — the official Salesforce exam-prep masterclass, Session 3. Covers business units + Salesforce CMS, Marketing Workspaces, and the eight data providers for content personalization.

cards.front: What two areas does Session 3 cover?
cards.back: 1) How Salesforce CMS integrates with Marketing Cloud Next (business units, workspaces, content). 2) The different options for content personalization (data providers, content variables, marketing objects, and personalization methods).
cards.frontHtml: What two areas does Session 3 cover?
cards.backHtml: 1) How Salesforce CMS integrates with Marketing Cloud Next (business units, workspaces, content). 2) The different options for content personalization (data providers, content variables, marketing objects, and personalization methods).

cards.front: What do business units separate in MC Next, and where is all marketing content stored?
cards.back: They separate content and data across teams, brands, or regions. All marketing content (images, landing pages, forms, brand assets, emails) is stored in CMS content workspaces .
cards.frontHtml: What do business units separate in MC Next, and where is all marketing content stored?
cards.backHtml: They separate content and data across teams, brands, or regions. All marketing content (images, landing pages, forms, brand assets, emails) is stored in CMS content workspaces.

cards.front: What is each CMS content workspace associated with?
cards.back: A specific business unit . This structure works alongside Data 360's data spaces .
cards.frontHtml: What is each CMS content workspace associated with?
cards.backHtml: A specific business unit. This structure works alongside Data 360's data spaces.

cards.front: What are the cardinalities between data spaces, business units, and content workspaces?
cards.back: A data space can be associated with no business units or one business unit . A business unit can be associated with one or more content workspaces .
cards.frontHtml: What are the cardinalities between data spaces, business units, and content workspaces?
cards.backHtml: A data space can be associated with no business units or one business unit. A business unit can be associated with one or more content workspaces.

cards.front: How does the system filter content by business unit?
cards.back: When marketers create an asset, the system displays only the content available to the associated business unit . The same filtering applies when selecting content from a campaign or flow .
cards.frontHtml: How does the system filter content by business unit?
cards.backHtml: When marketers create an asset, the system displays only the content available to the associated business unit. The same filtering applies when selecting content from a campaign or flow.

cards.front: Can content be accessed directly across business units?
cards.back: ⚠️ No — by design, content cannot be accessed directly across business units. Each CMS content workspace must be associated with a specific business unit in Setup.
cards.frontHtml: Can content be accessed directly across business units?
cards.backHtml: ⚠️ No — by design, content cannot be accessed directly across business units. Each CMS content workspace must be associated with a specific business unit in Setup.

cards.front: How do you share content across business units?
cards.back: Post content as a common asset , which makes it available to all business units . Users in other business units can then copy that asset into their own workspaces and use it locally.
cards.frontHtml: How do you share content across business units?
cards.backHtml: Post content as a common asset, which makes it available to all business units. Users in other business units can then copy that asset into their own workspaces and use it locally.

cards.front: What content access does each business unit role have?
cards.back: Marketing Standard = access to both the data space and CMS content . Marketing Read-Only = access to only the data space (no CMS content).
cards.frontHtml: What content access does each business unit role have?
cards.backHtml: Marketing Standard = access to both the data space and CMS content. Marketing Read-Only = access to only the data space (no CMS content).

cards.front: Who can only be assigned the Marketing Read-Only role?
cards.back: Users without the Marketing Manager or Marketing Admin permission sets.
cards.frontHtml: Who can only be assigned the Marketing Read-Only role?
cards.backHtml: Users without the Marketing Manager or Marketing Admin permission sets.

cards.front: What can you configure from a business unit's setup page?
cards.back: Associate CMS workspaces , assign authenticated email domains and channel-specific settings, configure preference pages for each domain , enable specific AI features , add members (with roles), and enable common assets (Business Unit Settings).
cards.frontHtml: What can you configure from a business unit's setup page?
cards.backHtml: Associate CMS workspaces, assign authenticated email domains and channel-specific settings, configure preference pages for each domain, enable specific AI features, add members (with roles), and enable common assets (Business Unit Settings).

cards.front: What is a Marketing Workspace, and how can you organise assets?
cards.back: Where content is stored. Use the default Marketing Cloud Content Workspace or create additional workspaces to organise assets by campaign, initiative, brand, or team — and to support collaboration across teams.
cards.frontHtml: What is a Marketing Workspace, and how can you organise assets?
cards.backHtml: Where content is stored. Use the default Marketing Cloud Content Workspace or create additional workspaces to organise assets by campaign, initiative, brand, or team — and to support collaboration across teams.

cards.front: How can content be shared between workspaces?
cards.back: Share content between marketing workspaces , or with a general workspace used by other users. Example: manage brand assets in a marketing workspace, then share them with a general workspace so other teams can use them.
cards.frontHtml: How can content be shared between workspaces?
cards.backHtml: Share content between marketing workspaces, or with a general workspace used by other users. Example: manage brand assets in a marketing workspace, then share them with a general workspace so other teams can use them.

cards.front: How do you organise and move content within/between workspaces?
cards.back: Organise content into folders within each workspace. Export content assets and import them into another Salesforce org — e.g., moving content between production and sandbox orgs.
cards.frontHtml: How do you organise and move content within/between workspaces?
cards.backHtml: Organise content into folders within each workspace. Export content assets and import them into another Salesforce org — e.g., moving content between production and sandbox orgs.

cards.front: Besides business-unit-level roles, how else can access be managed?
cards.back: By assigning roles at the individual workspace level .
cards.frontHtml: Besides business-unit-level roles, how else can access be managed?
cards.backHtml: By assigning roles at the individual workspace level.

cards.front: How do you create a Marketing Workspace?
cards.back: Content tab → Add Workspace → choose Marketing Workspace → enter a name and default language .
cards.frontHtml: How do you create a Marketing Workspace?
cards.backHtml: Content tab → Add Workspace → choose Marketing Workspace → enter a name and default language.

cards.front: Which content types should you be familiar with?
cards.back: The most commonly used: images, landing pages, forms, and emails . (MC Next supports many more, but you don't need to know all of them.)
cards.frontHtml: Which content types should you be familiar with?
cards.backHtml: The most commonly used: images, landing pages, forms, and emails. (MC Next supports many more, but you don't need to know all of them.)

cards.front: After saving content, what must happen before it can be used?
cards.back: It must be published . Saving alone isn't enough.
cards.frontHtml: After saving content, what must happen before it can be used?
cards.backHtml: It must be published. Saving alone isn't enough.

cards.front: Why must a form be created before a landing page?
cards.back: Because the form needs to exist before it can be placed on a page .
cards.frontHtml: Why must a form be created before a landing page?
cards.backHtml: Because the form needs to exist before it can be placed on a page.

cards.front: How do you set up a form's data source?
cards.back: Add a data source and choose the CRM object where submissions should create records (e.g., name it "leads" and select the Lead object).
cards.frontHtml: How do you set up a form's data source?
cards.backHtml: Add a data source and choose the CRM object where submissions should create records (e.g., name it "leads" and select the Lead object).

cards.front: What happens when you select "New Flow" on a form?
cards.back: It creates a form handler . Flow Builder pre-adds a Create Records element with mappings between the form fields and the corresponding record fields (e.g., Lead).
cards.frontHtml: What happens when you select "New Flow" on a form?
cards.backHtml: It creates a form handler. Flow Builder pre-adds a Create Records element with mappings between the form fields and the corresponding record fields (e.g., Lead).

cards.front: What happens when you publish a form?
cards.back: It also activates the associated flow .
cards.frontHtml: What happens when you publish a form?
cards.backHtml: It also activates the associated flow.

cards.front: What do you configure when building a landing page with a form?
cards.back: Add the published form , add other elements (e.g., a header image), configure the page title and SEO title , then save and publish . When a visitor submits the form, the flow runs and creates a new record in CRM.
cards.frontHtml: What do you configure when building a landing page with a form?
cards.backHtml: Add the published form, add other elements (e.g., a header image), configure the page title and SEO title, then save and publish. When a visitor submits the form, the flow runs and creates a new record in CRM.

cards.front: What is the primary data source for personalization in Marketing Cloud Engagement?
cards.back: Data extensions — either a sendable data extension (personalization strings reference subscriber data directly) or a non-sendable one (AMPscript retrieves the required fields). There are some exceptions, but data extensions remain primary.
cards.frontHtml: What is the primary data source for personalization in Marketing Cloud Engagement?
cards.backHtml: Data extensions — either a sendable data extension (personalization strings reference subscriber data directly) or a non-sendable one (AMPscript retrieves the required fields). There are some exceptions, but data extensions remain primary.

cards.front: What three mechanisms does MC Next offer for personalization?
cards.back: Data providers , content variables , and marketing objects .
cards.frontHtml: What three mechanisms does MC Next offer for personalization?
cards.backHtml: Data providers, content variables, and marketing objects.

cards.front: Which channel's personalization does the exam cover?
cards.back: Email content personalization only — not other channels.
cards.frontHtml: Which channel's personalization does the exam cover?
cards.backHtml: Email content personalization only — not other channels.

cards.front: What do merge fields do?
cards.back: Insert a single value from the selected data source into your content — the simplest option for field-level personalization .
cards.frontHtml: What do merge fields do?
cards.backHtml: Insert a single value from the selected data source into your content — the simplest option for field-level personalization.

cards.front: What do repeaters do?
cards.back: Display a collection of related items (recent purchases, upcoming events, recommended products). You design one item connected to a data source, and MC Next repeats that layout for each relevant record .
cards.frontHtml: What do repeaters do?
cards.backHtml: Display a collection of related items (recent purchases, upcoming events, recommended products). You design one item connected to a data source, and MC Next repeats that layout for each relevant record.

cards.front: What does dynamic content do?
cards.back: Changes an entire component or field based on targeting rules — the same email can show different images, offers, or messages depending on location, interests, or loyalty status. If a customer qualifies for multiple variations, you can prioritise which they see.
cards.frontHtml: What does dynamic content do?
cards.backHtml: Changes an entire component or field based on targeting rules — the same email can show different images, offers, or messages depending on location, interests, or loyalty status. If a customer qualifies for multiple variations, you can prioritise which they see.

cards.front: What does Handlebars provide?
cards.back: A templating language that can access nested data , apply conditional logic , format values , and iterate through collections — giving developers more control over how personalized content is rendered.
cards.frontHtml: What does Handlebars provide?
cards.backHtml: A templating language that can access nested data, apply conditional logic, format values, and iterate through collections — giving developers more control over how personalized content is rendered.

cards.front: What's the caveat about AMPscript in MC Next?
cards.back: You can use it for complex personalization logic and data operations, but ⚠️ not every AMPscript function available in Marketing Cloud Engagement is supported in Marketing Cloud Next .
cards.frontHtml: What's the caveat about AMPscript in MC Next?
cards.backHtml: You can use it for complex personalization logic and data operations, but ⚠️ not every AMPscript function available in Marketing Cloud Engagement is supported in Marketing Cloud Next.

cards.front: Which personalization methods are marketer-friendly vs. developer-oriented?
cards.back: Marketer configuration: merge fields, repeaters, dynamic content. Developer flexibility: Handlebars and AMPscript.
cards.frontHtml: Which personalization methods are marketer-friendly vs. developer-oriented?
cards.backHtml: Marketer configuration: merge fields, repeaters, dynamic content. Developer flexibility: Handlebars and AMPscript.

cards.front: Name the eight data providers in Marketing Cloud Next.
cards.back: 1) Data graph 2) Event 3) Activation 4) Salesforce record 5) Apex class 6) Personalization recommender 7) Lookup graph 8) Offer .
cards.frontHtml: Name the eight data providers in Marketing Cloud Next.
cards.backHtml: 1) Data graph 2) Event 3) Activation 4) Salesforce record 5) Apex class 6) Personalization recommender 7) Lookup graph 8) Offer.

cards.front: What is a data graph, and how does it work?
cards.back: A pre-assembled view combining selected fields from multiple related DMOs. It begins with a primary DMO (typically Individual or Unified Individual) and connects related objects (contact points, accounts, orders, products, engagement activity). Data 360 prepares it as a single read-only record , so MC Next retrieves customer data quickly without joining the underlying objects each time content is rendered .
cards.frontHtml: What is a data graph, and how does it work?
cards.backHtml: A pre-assembled view combining selected fields from multiple related DMOs. It begins with a primary DMO (typically Individual or Unified Individual) and connects related objects (contact points, accounts, orders, products, engagement activity). Data 360 prepares it as a single read-only record, so MC Next retrieves customer data quickly without joining the underlying objects each time content is rendered.

cards.front: What does an event data provider do, and what's its key limitation?
cards.back: It makes data from an event-triggered automation flow available for content. Each event has a defined schema corresponding to the underlying engagement DMO that triggers the flow (form submissions, email sends/opens, engagement signals). ⚠️ It supports direct attributes from the event DMO, but not related collections — e.g., an order event provides Sales Order DMO attributes but not related products from the Sales Order Product DMO.
cards.frontHtml: What does an event data provider do, and what's its key limitation?
cards.backHtml: It makes data from an event-triggered automation flow available for content. Each event has a defined schema corresponding to the underlying engagement DMO that triggers the flow (form submissions, email sends/opens, engagement signals). ⚠️ It supports direct attributes from the event DMO, but not related collections — e.g., an order event provides Sales Order DMO attributes but not related products from the Sales Order Product DMO.

cards.front: What does an activation data provider do?
cards.back: Makes the direct and related attributes configured in the activation available for content personalization. It supports segments based on either Individual or Unified Individual .
cards.frontHtml: What does an activation data provider do?
cards.backHtml: Makes the direct and related attributes configured in the activation available for content personalization. It supports segments based on either Individual or Unified Individual.

cards.front: Can a message use both an activation and an event data provider?
cards.back: ⚠️ No. Each requires a specific flow orchestration pattern, so using both would create a conflict in how the data is bound to the message .
cards.frontHtml: Can a message use both an activation and an event data provider?
cards.backHtml: ⚠️ No. Each requires a specific flow orchestration pattern, so using both would create a conflict in how the data is bound to the message.

cards.front: What does a Salesforce record data provider do?
cards.back: Lets you personalize content with current data from Salesforce CRM objects — add a case, lead, or another supported object as a data source, then insert its fields using merge fields.
cards.frontHtml: What does a Salesforce record data provider do?
cards.backHtml: Lets you personalize content with current data from Salesforce CRM objects — add a case, lead, or another supported object as a data source, then insert its fields using merge fields.

cards.front: What does an Apex class data provider do, and what is it designed for?
cards.back: It defines a custom data structure for personalization — the Apex class primarily defines the schema (fields and data types) that content can reference. It's designed for on-demand or broadcast flows passing data into an email, but can be used with other flow types.
cards.frontHtml: What does an Apex class data provider do, and what is it designed for?
cards.backHtml: It defines a custom data structure for personalization — the Apex class primarily defines the schema (fields and data types) that content can reference. It's designed for on-demand or broadcast flows passing data into an email, but can be used with other flow types.

cards.front: What does a personalization recommender do?
cards.back: Brings recommendations from Salesforce Personalization into an email — returning a collection of relevant products, services, or content per recipient, displayed using a Repeater component.
cards.frontHtml: What does a personalization recommender do?
cards.backHtml: Brings recommendations from Salesforce Personalization into an email — returning a collection of relevant products, services, or content per recipient, displayed using a Repeater component.

cards.front: What does a lookup graph data provider do?
cards.back: Provides access to non-profile data that doesn't have a direct relationship back to a unified individual. It takes a value from the recipient's primary data graph and uses it as a key to retrieve matching information from a second, smaller data graph (e.g., a product identifier → product details from a catalog graph). Results display in merge fields or repeaters.
cards.frontHtml: What does a lookup graph data provider do?
cards.backHtml: Provides access to non-profile data that doesn't have a direct relationship back to a unified individual. It takes a value from the recipient's primary data graph and uses it as a key to retrieve matching information from a second, smaller data graph (e.g., a product identifier → product details from a catalog graph). Results display in merge fields or repeaters.

cards.front: What does the offer data provider do?
cards.back: Works with Salesforce Loyalty Management to deliver tailored promotions in email content. Use merge fields for offer name/description/coupon code, and dynamic content rules to show different offers by customer attribute (e.g., loyalty tier).
cards.frontHtml: What does the offer data provider do?
cards.backHtml: Works with Salesforce Loyalty Management to deliver tailored promotions in email content. Use merge fields for offer name/description/coupon code, and dynamic content rules to show different offers by customer attribute (e.g., loyalty tier).

cards.front: What are content variables, and how do they differ from a data graph?
cards.back: Custom placeholders defined within an email and populated at runtime from Salesforce Flow . Unlike a data graph, they don't retrieve data from predefined customer data structures — the email defines what it expects (order number, appointment date, discount amount, support rep's name) and the flow supplies the values at send time.
cards.frontHtml: What are content variables, and how do they differ from a data graph?
cards.backHtml: Custom placeholders defined within an email and populated at runtime from Salesforce Flow. Unlike a data graph, they don't retrieve data from predefined customer data structures — the email defines what it expects (order number, appointment date, discount amount, support rep's name) and the flow supplies the values at send time.

cards.front: What can a content variable be mapped to?
cards.back: Any data source available to Salesforce Flow — including Salesforce data, MuleSoft integrations, and HTTP connectors. Useful when information is calculated during the flow or comes from a system outside Data 360 .
cards.frontHtml: What can a content variable be mapped to?
cards.backHtml: Any data source available to Salesforce Flow — including Salesforce data, MuleSoft integrations, and HTTP connectors. Useful when information is calculated during the flow or comes from a system outside Data 360.

cards.front: What data types do content variables support?
cards.back: Boolean, Text, Date, DateTime, and Number — plus a Record ID value that references a Salesforce record.
cards.frontHtml: What data types do content variables support?
cards.backHtml: Boolean, Text, Date, DateTime, and Number — plus a Record ID value that references a Salesforce record.

cards.front: In simple terms, how do content variables work?
cards.back: The content defines the placeholders , and the flow supplies their values at send time .
cards.frontHtml: In simple terms, how do content variables work?
cards.backHtml: The content defines the placeholders, and the flow supplies their values at send time.

cards.front: What is a marketing object, and what's the MCE comparison?
cards.back: A flexible data store in MC Next holding information for marketing use cases. The closest MCE comparison is a data extension .

cards.front: What are marketing objects useful for storing?
cards.back: Product catalogs, reference tables, rewards balances, promotional codes, and more.
cards.frontHtml: What are marketing objects useful for storing?

cards.front: Why do marketing objects give marketers autonomy?
cards.back: Because an admin doesn't need to create a Salesforce object or modify the Data 360 data model — a marketer creates one by importing a CSV, defining fields, and identifying a primary key.
cards.frontHtml: Why do marketing objects give marketers autonomy?

cards.front: How do you use marketing object data in a message?
cards.back: Query the marketing object with Handlebars or AMPscript . Example: use the recipient's address from the default data graph to find their matching record in a marketing object and retrieve their current rewards balance.
cards.frontHtml: How do you use marketing object data in a message?

cards.front: What field types do marketing objects support, and how is data refreshed?
cards.back: Text, number, and decimal fields. Data can be fully refreshed by uploading a new CSV file, which replaces existing records .
cards.frontHtml: What field types do marketing objects support, and how is data refreshed?
cards.backHtml: Text, number, and decimal fields. Data can be fully refreshed by uploading a new CSV file, which replaces existing records.

cards.front: In summary, what is a marketing object?
cards.back: A marketer-managed table of data that can be queried at runtime to personalize content.

cards.front: How do you create a marketing object?

cards.frontHtml: How do you create a marketing object?
cards.backHtml: From the Data Management tab in the Marketing app → New → upload a CSV → Next → give it a name → review the fields and data types detected from the file (adjust if needed) → select the primary key field → done.

cards.front: What can you define when inserting a merge field?
cards.back: A fallback value to use when the customer's data is missing (e.g., "Friend" when the first name is absent). The merge field menu shows the configured data providers alongside options like global strings .
cards.frontHtml: What can you define when inserting a merge field?
cards.backHtml: A fallback value to use when the customer's data is missing (e.g., "Friend" when the first name is absent). The merge field menu shows the configured data providers alongside options like global strings.

cards.front: What two levels of personalization does the back-in-stock demo illustrate?
cards.back: Merge fields provide a simple, marketer-friendly way to insert data; Handlebars and AMPscript give more control over how data is retrieved and formatted (e.g., converting a name to uppercase, formatting a price as currency).

cards.front: What does dynamic content require?

cards.front: Walk through the US West States variation demo.
cards.back: Select the header image → in the dynamic content section of the image properties panel click New Variation → name it → define the targeting rule by selecting the State/Province field from the individual's related contact point address data → choose the isIn operator → enter the state values → save → assign a different header image. You can preview each variation, create more, and set priority order when a recipient qualifies for multiple.
